tagline: Follow the Farmington to an axe factory and its surviving sluices.
intro: Routes 4 and 179 follow the Farmington River toward Collinsville, where the road crosses the river beside the village’s industrial landscape. The 2.02-mile Route 4 section between Perry Street and Route 179 received state scenic-road designation in 2013. A scenic section of Route 179 continues through Canton from the Burlington town line to SR 565. The river also powered Collinsville’s axe factory: its water turned turbines that drove the machines, and old factory buildings remain beside the channels that carried it through the works.

The river road once carried a different number. In 1922, the connection between Collinsville and Farmington center became State Highway 138; it became part of Route 4 in 1932. The earlier Route 4 had approached Collinsville from Torrington on what is now Route 202, then turned south along today’s Route 179 toward Unionville. When Route 4 was realigned in 1963, its former Canton-to-Burlington section became Route 179.

From Perry Street, take Route 4 west to Route 179 in Burlington, then follow Route 179 north along the river into Canton and across it at Collinsville. The Collins Company’s factory buildings remain along the riverbanks, threaded by the sluices of the former water-powered works.

moments.title: Route 179
moments.text: The turn north at Burlington follows a former piece of Route 4. Route 179 acquired this stretch in 1963, when Route 4 was realigned. From its junction with Route 4, the highway follows the Farmington River into Canton, then crosses the river in Collinsville. Its scenic-road designation covers the Canton section between the Burlington town line and SR 565. The numbered highway continues beyond the village, meeting US 202 and US 44 before following Cherry Brook through Canton Center. Route 179 ultimately reaches East Hartland, where it ends at Route 20.

moments.title: Collinsville
moments.text: Sluices weave through the old factory buildings along the Farmington, marking the water-powered works around which Collinsville grew. River water turned turbines and powered machines that made edge tools, including axes, machetes, picks and knives. The company closed in 1966, but its buildings survived. One building, erected in 1865 to finish and assemble agricultural plows, became an employee recreation facility in 1924 and now houses the Canton Historical Museum. Pattern maker Fred Widen used part of it for his collection of Collins memorabilia. The historical society now owns the building, whose collections include Collins tools, agricultural equipment and looms.
moments.notice: The factory buildings along the riverbanks are interwoven with sluices.

moments.title: Town Bridge
moments.text: Iron cresting decorates the entrance portals of Town Bridge, north of Collinsville. The Berlin Iron Bridge Company built it in 1895 as part of a town program to improve crossings of the flood-prone Farmington River. Its single Parker truss span uses pinned connections, a method that gave way to rivets by about 1900. Riveted connections are also present on the structure. The bridge stands on Town Bridge Road, about 0.1 miles west of Route 179, making it a separate excursion beyond the village. Its span measures about 172 feet, with a metal deck covered in asphalt.
moments.notice: Look at the iron cresting above the bridge’s entrance portals.
